messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adaeze is a 74-year-old woman of Nigerian heritage who has lived in a rural farming community in the American South for most of her adult life. She works the land alongside a small cooperative of neighbors, tending vegetable plots from early morning until the heat of the day forces her indoors. She has been in a long-term relationship for over two decades, though her partner has noticed, with growing concern, that she has become increasingly unreachable. Adaeze came to the attention of a clinical psychologist after her primary care physician, alarmed by her score of 65 on the PCL-5 and by her quiet admission that she was no longer certain her life was worth living, made an urgent referral.

The assault occurred approximately three years ago, in the early morning hours before dawn, when Adaeze was alone in the fields preparing the soil for a late planting. The silence that morning had been total — no birdsong, no wind, just the dark and the smell of turned earth — when a man she did not know attacked her from behind. The rape was brutal and prolonged. She was left on the ground, her hands still in the soil, the smell of it filling her lungs. She did not tell anyone for several weeks.

The fields where Adaeze has worked for decades have become a landscape of ambush. The rich, loamy smell of soil — once a source of quiet satisfaction — now arrives before memory does, pulling her back to the ground before she has time to prepare herself. On the anniversary of the assault each year, she has found herself unable to leave her bed, the date itself functioning as a kind of alarm her body sounds without her permission. And silence — particularly the sudden, complete silence that settles over the fields at certain hours — strikes her with a physical force, as though the absence of sound is itself a warning. When these triggers arrive, Adaeze has learned to respond immediately: she forces herself to think only positive thoughts, rehearsing gratitudes and blessings in a kind of internal recitation, and she avoids any circumstance that might carry her back — she no longer works in the dark, she has stopped entering certain parts of the field, and she has withdrawn from any form of physical contact with others, including her partner.

Yet the triggers do not merely provoke her strategies; they also confirm her worst beliefs about herself. When the smell of earth floods her, she does not only see the memory — she feels, in that moment, that her body is contaminated, that something has been permanently soiled in her. She has come to believe that what happened to her body was a kind of defilement she carries still, and this shame is not abstract but visceral, arriving alongside every sensory reminder of that morning. The appraisals themselves, once established, have taken on a life that reaches back toward the triggers: on the anniversary, she does not simply grieve — she finds herself scanning the silence of the house, alert to any absence of sound, her body already rehearsing the fear that belongs to the field. The belief that she is contaminated makes the smell of soil unbearable in ways that go beyond memory, because the smell no longer only recalls the event — it confirms the conclusion she has already drawn about herself.

The strategies she has adopted to manage this have quietly worsened her situation. Avoiding touch has meant that her partner's attempts at comfort are met with withdrawal, and the relational distance this has created has left Adaeze feeling more isolated and, in her own words, more broken — reinforcing her sense that her life may no longer hold sufficient meaning. Forcing positive thoughts has prevented her from processing what happened, and in the moments when the effort fails — when a smell or a silence breaks through — the intrusion feels more violent for having been suppressed, and the shame returns with renewed force. The avoidance of dark or field-adjacent circumstances has narrowed her world to the point where her occupation, the central source of identity and routine in her life, has become a daily negotiation with terror. Her coworkers have noticed her leaving early, her partner has stopped reaching for her hand, and Adaeze herself has arrived at the clinic exhausted — hoping, she said quietly, that someone might help her feel clean again.
